title: Utah & BYU Game Kickoff Times Shifted After Ground Stop, FOX 13 Reports
body:
The University of Utah’s Saturday matchup against Arizona and Brigham Young University’s game later in the day will both start later than originally scheduled after a nationwide “ground stop” forced the cancellation of hundreds of flights on Friday, leaving the Utes stranded in Salt Lake City and prompting the Pac‑12 to shift kickoff times to accommodate travel disruptions.

The unexpected aviation shutdown, ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration in response to a severe weather system that swept across the western United States, grounded commercial and private aircraft from the Rockies to the Pacific Coast. While the storm itself has moved eastward, its ripple effects are still being felt in the inter‑mountain region, where airlines have struggled to re‑schedule flights and clear backlogs of delayed passengers. Utah’s football team, which was slated to depart for Tucson on Friday night, found its travel plans upended, forcing the program to remain in Salt Lake City overnight.

In response, the Pac‑12 announced that Utah’s game against the Arizona Wildcats will now tip‑off at 5:30 p.m. Mountain Time, roughly an hour later than the original 4:30 p.m. start. BYU, which was set to travel to Provo for its own contest, will see its kickoff pushed back to 7:00 p.m., allowing the Cougars additional time to coordinate ground transportation and accommodate players who are still awaiting re‑booked flights. The league’s decision reflects a growing trend among major sports organizations to prioritize athlete safety and logistical feasibility when external factors—particularly weather‑related travel disruptions—interfere with scheduled events.

Coaches from both programs expressed relief that the games will still be played, while also acknowledging the challenges the delay creates. Utah head coach Kyle Whittingham said, “Our guys have been ready to go, and while the travel hiccup is frustrating, we appreciate the conference’s flexibility. We’ll use the extra time to fine‑tune our game plan and make sure the players stay focused.” BYU’s Kyle Whittingham (no relation) echoed similar sentiments, noting that the team’s preparation routine will be adjusted but the core of the game plan remains unchanged. Both coaching staffs emphasized that the athletes’ health and safety remain the top priority, especially after a long travel day that could have left players fatigued.

The ripple effect of the ground stop extends beyond the two Utah‑based programs. Several other Pac‑12 schools, including Colorado and Oregon State, reported minor schedule tweaks as airlines worked to restore normal operations. Ticket holders for the Utes‑Wildcats game have been notified of the new start time via email and text alerts, and stadium officials are coordinating with local transit agencies to ensure fans can still reach the Arizona Stadium in time for the later kickoff. Meanwhile, BYU’s fan base in Provo is being urged to arrive earlier than usual to avoid traffic congestion that could be exacerbated by the delayed start.

Analysts point out that the situation underscores the vulnerability of college football’s tightly packed schedule to unforeseen disruptions. With conference championships and bowl selections looming, any delay can have cascading consequences for team preparation, television contracts, and revenue streams. The Pac‑12’s swift adjustment demonstrates an increasing willingness to adapt, but it also raises questions about contingency planning for future weather events. Some experts suggest that conferences might consider building buffer windows into their scheduling or establishing dedicated travel contingency funds to mitigate similar scenarios.

Looking ahead, both Utah and BYU will need to quickly regroup and refocus on their respective opponents. Utah’s road trip to Tucson will now involve a tighter turnaround, as the team must travel back to Salt Lake City after the game and prepare for its next outing. BYU, meanwhile, will have a shortened recovery period before its subsequent conference matchup. Fans can expect both teams to lean on their depth and resilience, traits that have become hallmarks of mountain‑state programs. As the weather clears and flights resume normal service, the broader college football landscape will be watching to see how quickly the logistical fallout from the ground stop dissipates and whether any long‑term scheduling reforms emerge from this week’s disruption.
